1	---
     2	name: file-reading
     3	description: "Use this skill when a file has been uploaded but its content is NOT in your context — only its path at /mnt/user-data/uploads/ is listed in an uploaded_files block. This skill is a router: it tells you which tool to use for each file type (pdf, docx, xlsx, csv, json, images, archives, ebooks) so you read the right amount the right way instead of blindly running cat on a binary. Triggers: any mention of /mnt/user-data/uploads/, an uploaded_files section, a file_path tag, or a user asking about an uploaded file you have not yet read. Do NOT use this skill if the file content is already visible in your context inside a documents block — you already have it."
     4	compatibility: "claude.ai, Claude Desktop, Cowork — any surface where uploads land at /mnt/user-data/uploads/"
     5	license: Proprietary. LICENSE.txt has complete terms
     6	---
     7	
     8	# Reading Uploaded Files
     9	
    10	## Why this skill exists
    11	
    12	When a user uploads a file in claude.ai, Claude Desktop, or Cowork,
    13	the file is written to `/mnt/user-data/uploads/<filename>` and you are told the path
    14	in an `<uploaded_files>` block. **The content is not in your context.**
    15	You must go read it.
    16	
    17	The naive thing — `cat /mnt/user-data/uploads/whatever` — is wrong for
    18	most files:
    19	
    20	- On a PDF it prints binary garbage.
    21	- On a 100MB CSV it floods your context with rows you will never use.
    22	- On a DOCX it prints the raw ZIP bytes.
    23	- On an image it does nothing useful at all.
    24	
    25	This skill tells you the right first move for each type, and when to
    26	hand off to a deeper skill.
    27	
    28	## General protocol
    29	
    30	1. **Look at the extension.** That is your dispatch key.
    31	2. **Stat before you read.** Large files need sampling, not slurping.
    32	   ```bash
    33	   stat -c '%s bytes, %y' /mnt/user-data/uploads/report.pdf
    34	   file /mnt/user-data/uploads/report.pdf
    35	   ```
    36	3. **Read just enough to answer the user's question.** If they asked
    37	   "how many rows are in this CSV", don't load the whole thing into
    38	   pandas — `wc -l` gives a fast approximation (it counts newlines,
    39	   not CSV records, so it may over-count if quoted fields contain
    40	   embedded newlines).
    41	4. **If a dedicated skill exists, go read it.** The table below tells
    42	   you when. The dedicated skills cover editing, creating, and advanced
    43	   operations that this skill does not.
    44	
    45	## `extract-text`
    46	
    47	For docx, odt, epub, xlsx, pptx, rtf, and ipynb the first move is
    48	`extract-text <file>`. It emits markdown for docx/odt/epub (headings,
    49	bold, lists, links, tables), tab-separated rows under `## Sheet:`
    50	headers for xlsx, text under `## Slide N` headers for pptx, fenced
    51	code cells for ipynb, and plain text for rtf. Pass `--format <fmt>`
    52	when the extension is wrong or absent (e.g., `--format xlsx` on an
    53	`.xlsm`). If it errors on a file, `pandoc <file> -t plain` is a
    54	fallback; for xlsx/pptx, fall back to the dedicated skill's
    55	Python-based approach (openpyxl / python-pptx).
    56	
    57	## Dispatch table
    58	
    59	Where a dedicated skill is named below, invoke it by name if you have a
    60	Skill tool, or Read its SKILL.md (listed in your available skills, or in
    61	the same skills directory as this file).
    62	
    63	| Extension                         | First move                                           | Dedicated skill |
    64	| --------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- | --------------- |
    65	| `.pdf`                            | Content inventory (see PDF section)                  | `pdf-reading`   |
    66	| `.docx`                           | `extract-text`                                       | `docx`          |
    67	| `.doc` (legacy)                   | Convert to `.docx` first                             | `docx`          |
    68	| `.xlsx`                           | `extract-text`                                       | `xlsx`          |
    69	| `.xlsm`                           | `extract-text --format xlsx`                         | `xlsx`          |
    70	| `.xls` (legacy)                   | `pd.read_excel(engine="xlrd")` — openpyxl rejects it | `xlsx`          |
    71	| `.ods`                            | `pd.read_excel(engine="odf")` — openpyxl rejects it  | `xlsx`          |
    72	| `.pptx`                           | `extract-text`                                       | `pptx`          |
    73	| `.ppt` (legacy)                   | Convert to `.pptx` first                             | `pptx`          |
    74	| `.csv`, `.tsv`                    | `pandas` with `nrows`                                | — (below)       |
    75	| `.json`, `.jsonl`                 | `jq` for structure                                   | — (below)       |
    76	| `.jpg`, `.png`, `.gif`, `.webp`   | Already in your context as vision input              | — (below)       |
    77	| `.zip`, `.tar`, `.tar.gz`         | List contents, do **not** auto-extract               | — (below)       |
    78	| `.gz` (single file)               | `zcat \| head` — no manifest to list                 | — (below)       |
    79	| `.epub`, `.odt`                   | `extract-text`                                       | — (below)       |
    80	| `.rtf`                            | `extract-text`                                       | — (below)       |
    81	| `.ipynb`                          | `extract-text`                                       | — (below)       |
    82	| `.txt`, `.md`, `.log`, code files | `wc -c` then `head` or full `cat`                    | — (below)       |
    83	| Unknown                           | `file` then decide                                   | —               |
    84	
    85	---
    86	
    87	## PDF
    88	
    89	**Never** `cat` a PDF — it prints binary garbage.
    90	
    91	Quick first move — get the page count and determine whether the PDF
    92	has an extractable text layer:
    93	
    94	```bash
    95	pdfinfo /mnt/user-data/uploads/report.pdf
    96	pdffonts /mnt/user-data/uploads/report.pdf
    97	```
    98	
    99	`pdffonts` tells you whether text extraction will work before you try it:
   100	
   101	- **No fonts listed** (empty table, just the header) → the PDF is a
   102	  scan or raster export. `pdftotext` and `PdfReader.extract_text()`
   103	  will return nothing useful. Go straight to page rasterization or OCR
   104	  — see the `pdf-reading` skill → "Scanned documents".
   105	- **Fonts listed** → there is a text layer; extract it:
   106	  ```bash
   107	  pdftotext -f 1 -l 1 /mnt/user-data/uploads/report.pdf - | head -20
   108	  ```
   109	
   110	The reason to check `pdffonts` first is user-facing: running
   111	`pdftotext` on a scan produces an empty result, and in a visible
   112	transcript that reads as a failed first attempt before you fall back
   113	to OCR. The two-line diagnostic above costs one tool call and avoids
   114	that — you arrive at the right method on the first try, which is what
   115	a user perceives as "it just read my file."
   116	
   117	That also shapes how to open your reply. The diagnostic commands are
   118	plumbing, not content; lead with what the user asked about. On a
   119	scanned receipt that might be "This is a 3-page scanned invoice; the
   120	amount due on page 2 is $1,845.00," and on a digitally-authored report
   121	it might be "The Q3 report runs 28 pages; revenue on p. 4 is $12.3M,
   122	up 9% YoY." What you're steering away from is the "I'll examine the
   123	PDF" / "Let me check if this is extractable" preamble — the answer to
   124	their question is the first thing they should see.
   125	
   126	For anything beyond a quick peek — figures, tables, attachments,
   127	forms, scanned PDFs, visual inspection, or choosing a reading strategy
   128	— go read the `pdf-reading` skill. It covers content inventory, text
   129	extraction vs. page rasterization, embedded content extraction, and
   130	document-type-aware reading strategies.
   131	
   132	For PDF form filling, creation, merging, splitting, or watermarking,
   133	go read the `pdf` skill.
   134	
   135	---
   136	
   137	## DOCX / DOC
   138	
   139	The `docx` skill covers editing, creating, tracked changes, images.
   140	Read it if you need any of those. For a quick look:
   141	
   142	```bash
   143	extract-text /mnt/user-data/uploads/memo.docx | head -200
   144	```
   145	
   146	Legacy `.doc` (not `.docx`) must be converted first — see the `docx`
   147	skill.
   148	
   149	---
   150	
   151	## XLSX / XLS / spreadsheets
   152	
   153	The `xlsx` skill covers formulas, formatting, charts, creating. Read
   154	it if you need any of those. For a quick look at an `.xlsx`:
   155	
   156	```bash
   157	extract-text /mnt/user-data/uploads/data.xlsx | head -100
   158	```
   159	
   160	For `.xlsm`, add `--format xlsx` (same zip structure; only the
   161	extension differs). When you need a structured preview in Python:
   162	
   163	```python
   164	from openpyxl import load_workbook
   165	wb = load_workbook("/mnt/user-data/uploads/data.xlsx", read_only=True)
   166	print("Sheets:", wb.sheetnames)
   167	ws = wb.active
   168	for row in ws.iter_rows(max_row=5, values_only=True):
   169	    print(row)
   170	```
   171	
   172	`read_only=True` matters — without it, openpyxl loads the entire
   173	workbook into memory, which breaks on large files. Do not trust
   174	`ws.max_row` in read-only mode: many non-Excel writers omit the
   175	dimension record, so it comes back `None` or wrong. If you need a row
   176	count, iterate or use pandas.
   177	
   178	**Legacy `.xls`** — openpyxl raises `InvalidFileException`. Use:
   179	
   180	```python
   181	import pandas as pd
   182	df = pd.read_excel("/mnt/user-data/uploads/old.xls", engine="xlrd", nrows=5)
   183	```
   184	
   185	**`.ods` (OpenDocument)** — openpyxl also rejects this. Use:
   186	
   187	```python
   188	import pandas as pd
   189	df = pd.read_excel("/mnt/user-data/uploads/data.ods", engine="odf", nrows=5)
   190	```
   191	
   192	---
   193	
   194	## PPTX
   195	
   196	```bash
   197	extract-text /mnt/user-data/uploads/deck.pptx | head -200
   198	```
   199	
   200	**Legacy `.ppt`** — convert to `.pptx` first via LibreOffice; see the
   201	`pptx` skill for the sandbox-safe `scripts/office/soffice.py` wrapper
   202	(bare `soffice` hangs here because the seccomp filter blocks the
   203	`AF_UNIX` sockets LibreOffice uses for instance management).
   204	
   205	For anything beyond reading, go to the `pptx` skill.
   206	
   207	---
   208	
   209	## CSV / TSV
   210	
   211	**Do not** `cat` or `head` these blindly. A CSV with a 50KB quoted cell
   212	in row 1 will wreck your `head -5`. Use pandas with `nrows`:
   213	
   214	```python
   215	import pandas as pd
   216	df = pd.read_csv("/mnt/user-data/uploads/data.csv", nrows=5)
   217	print(df)
   218	print()
   219	print(df.dtypes)
   220	```
   221	
   222	Approximate row count without loading (over-counts if the file has
   223	RFC-4180 quoted newlines — the same quoted-cell case this section
   224	warned about above):
   225	
   226	```bash
   227	wc -l /mnt/user-data/uploads/data.csv
   228	```
   229

   232	```python

   234	print(df.describe())
   235	```
   236	
   237	TSV: same, with `sep="\t"`.
   238	
   239	---
   240	
   241	## JSON / JSONL
   242	
   243	Structure first, content second:
   244	
   245	```bash

   247	jq 'if type == "array" then length elif type == "object" then keys else . end' /mnt/user-data/uploads/data.json
   248	```
   249	
   250	(`keys` errors on scalar JSON roots — a bare `"hello"` or `42` is valid
   251	JSON per RFC 7159 — so guard the branch.)
   252

   254	
   255	JSONL (one object per line) — do **not** `jq` the whole file; work line
   256	by line:

   258	```bash

   261	```
   262	
   263	---
   264	
   265	## Images (JPG / PNG / GIF / WEBP)
   266	
   267	**You can already see uploaded images.** They are injected into your
   268	context as vision inputs alongside the `<uploaded_files>` pointer. You
   269	do not need to read them from disk to describe them.

   271	The disk copy is only needed if you are going to **process** the image
   272	programmatically:
   273	
   274	```python
   275	from PIL import Image
   276	img = Image.open("/mnt/user-data/uploads/photo.jpg")
   277	print(img.size, img.mode, img.format)
   278	```
   279	
   280	For OCR on an image (text extraction, not description):
   281	
   282	```python
   283	import pytesseract
   284	print(pytesseract.image_to_string(img))
   285	```
   286	
   287	Note: the client resizes images larger than 2000×2000 down to that
   288	bound and re-encodes as JPEG before upload, so the disk copy may not
   289	be the user's original bytes. For most processing this doesn't matter;
   290	if the user is asking about original-resolution pixel data, flag it.
   291	
   292	---
   293	
   294	## Archives (ZIP / TAR / TAR.GZ)
   295	
   296	**List first. Extract never — unless the user explicitly asks.**
   297	Archives can be huge, contain path traversal, or nest forever.
   298	
   299	```bash
   300	unzip -l /mnt/user-data/uploads/bundle.zip
   301	tar -tf /mnt/user-data/uploads/bundle.tar
   302	```
   303	
   304	GNU tar auto-detects compression — `tar -tf` works on `.tar`,
   305	`.tar.gz`, `.tar.bz2`, `.tar.xz` alike. Don't hard-code `-z`.
   306	
   307	If the user wants one file from inside, extract just that one:
   308	
   309	```bash
   310	unzip -p /mnt/user-data/uploads/bundle.zip path/inside/file.txt
   311	```
   312	
   313	**Standalone `.gz`** (not a tar) compresses a single file — there is
   314	no manifest to list. Just peek at the decompressed content:
   315	
   316	```bash
   317	zcat /mnt/user-data/uploads/data.json.gz | head -50
   318	```
   319	
   320	---
   321	
   322	## EPUB / ODT
   323	
   324	```bash
   325	extract-text /mnt/user-data/uploads/book.epub | head -200
   326	```
   327	
   328	For long ebooks, pipe through `head` — you rarely need the whole thing
   329	to answer a question.
   330	
   331	---
   332	
   333	## RTF / IPYNB
   334	
   335	```bash
   336	extract-text /mnt/user-data/uploads/notes.rtf | head -200
   337	extract-text /mnt/user-data/uploads/notebook.ipynb | head -200
   338	```
   339	
   340	---
   341	
   342	## Plain text / code / logs
   343	
   344	Check the size first:
   345	
   346	```bash
   347	wc -c /mnt/user-data/uploads/app.log
   348	```
   349	
   350	- **Under ~20KB**: `cat` is fine.
   351	- **Over ~20KB**: `head -100` and `tail -100` to orient. If the user
   352	  asked about something specific, `grep` for it. Load the whole thing
   353	  only if you genuinely need all of it.
   354	
   355	For log files, the user almost always cares about the end:
   356	
   357	```bash

   359	```
   360	
   361	---
   362	
   363	## Unknown extension
   364	
   365	```bash
   366	file /mnt/user-data/uploads/mystery.bin
   367	xxd /mnt/user-data/uploads/mystery.bin | head -5
   368	```
   369	
   370	`file` identifies most things. `xxd` head shows magic bytes. If `file`
   371	says "data" and the hex doesn't match anything you recognize, ask the
   372	user what it is instead of guessing.

import re, hashlib, sys
sys.path.insert(0,'.')
txt=open('BUILD62_compendia.md','rb').read().decode('utf-8')
lines=txt.split('\n')
heads=["Transitions compose","The six axes of the tower","Three excluded forms",
"Law versus extent, and what E measures","An index whose one prediction is false",
"The occupancy clock, and definability is not reachability","The arrow is a property of the assumption",
"The arrows decay with distance","Past, present and future","Exactness proves the three parts are not a triangle",
"Two indices, and the one that does not exist","Every stage of the tower in one table",
"The fourteenth axis, and the tower's last stage","How Λ enters a larger index"]
ok=True; n_ok=0
print("--- 14 tower headings (exact heading-line matches) ---")
for h in heads:
    hits=[i+1 for i,l in enumerate(lines) if l.strip()=="### "+h]
    st = "PASS" if len(hits)==1 else "FAIL"
    if st=="PASS": n_ok+=1
    else: ok=False
    print(f"{st} {len(hits)}x L{hits} {h}")
print(f"headings present exactly once: {n_ok}/14")
print("--- MC-33 / MC-34 tokens ---")
for tok in ["0.283507","0.302400","[3, 23]"]:
    c=txt.count(tok); print(("PASS" if c>=1 else "FAIL"), repr(tok), "count", c)
    if c<1: ok=False
print("--- Λ8 rebuild + §7.4 caps ---")
from lam8 import L8, L9
cells=L8(); edges=L9()
print("|Λ8| =",len(cells),"|Λ9| =",len(edges))
names=['n','l','k','q','e','f','g','2S']
mx={nm:max(c[i] for c in cells) for i,nm in enumerate(names)}
mn={nm:min(c[i] for c in cells) for i,nm in enumerate(names)}
caps=(mx['n'],mx['e'],mx['l'],mx['k'],mx['f'])
box=1
for nm in names: box*= (mx[nm]-mn[nm]+1)
void=box-len(cells)
print("caps (n,e,l,k,f) =",caps, "PASS" if caps==(3,3,1,3,1) else "FAIL")
print("box =",box,"PASS" if box==6912 else "FAIL", "| void =",void,"PASS" if void==5936 else "FAIL")
print("ranges:",{nm:(mn[nm],mx[nm]) for nm in names})
if not (len(cells)==976 and len(edges)==1654 and caps==(3,3,1,3,1) and box==6912 and void==5936): ok=False
print("\nSEGMENT-3 RESULT:", "PASS" if ok else "FAIL")
EOF

{"returncode":0,"stdout":"3544: ### 12.11.8 The electromagnetic index, and it was inside Λ all along
3545: 
3546:  A cell of Λ is called a transition, and a transition is not an atomic event — it is an
3547:  electromagnetic one. Whether a photon connects two configurations is decided by multipolarity,
3548:  parity and the angular momentum the field carries. **None of that is a coordinate of Λ. All of it is
3549:  a function of Λ's coordinates.**
3550: 
3551:  **What Λ supplies, and what it does not.** Λ's cells give a source (n, ℓ, k, 2S) and a target
3552:  (e, f, g, 2S′, v, 2J_c, 2K, 2J). **There is no source J** — the tower builds J on the target side
3553:  only. So exactly two electromagnetic quantities are available:
3554: 
3555:     Δℓ = f − ℓ      at Λ₈        ΔS = 2S′ − 2S      at Λ₉
3556: 
3557:  and |ΔJ| is available at no level of the tower. The multipole is therefore determined by Δℓ and
3558:  parity alone: **Δℓ = 0 → M1, Δℓ = 1 → E1, Δℓ = 2 → E2, Δℓ = 3 → E3**, the lowest whose parity
3559:  matches. The map was validated against nine textbook classifications before use and shown able to
3560:  refuse, per §4.6.
3561: 
3562:  **The image, and it is a rectangle.** All 1,654 cells of Λ₉ map, onto eight cells:
3563: 
3564:   multipole   ΔS = 0   ΔS = 1   ΔS = 2   ΔS = 3
3565:   E1             264      342      180       54
3566:   M1             262      337      171       44
3567: 
3568:  **E = 0, and the zero is worth nothing**, because the image is the complete product — 2 × 4 here,
3569:  and 4 × 11 at caps (5,5,3,10,3). Register 333's warning, in a new place: a closure test passes on a
3570:  full box for free. **What the rectangle says is that Δℓ and ΔS are independent in Λ: every multipole
3571:  occurs with every spin change.**
3572: 
3573:     **Λ imposes no electromagnetic constraint at all.** 576 of its Λ₉ cells are E1
3574:     transitions with ΔS ≠ 0 — intercombination lines, which LS coupling forbids.
3575: 
3576:  **Half the missing law can be imposed and half cannot**, and §17.3's criterion says which in advance:
3577: 
3578:   rule                as a set                convex in range?   imposed on Λ₉
3579:   ΔS = 0, spin        σ⁻¹({0})                **yes**            526 cells, **E = 0**
3580:   |Δℓ| = 1, parity    δ⁻¹({−1, +1})           **no, hole at 0**  840 cells, **E = 750**
3581: 
3582:  and the spin rule holds at four cap settings — 1,654, 2,664, 44,153 and 60,164 cells, E = 0 at each.
3583:  **The parity rule is the fourth instance of §12.11.2's second excluded form**, and the first for
3584:  which the criterion names the repair that would work: any reparametrisation moving the hole to an
3585:  endpoint.
3586: 
3587:  **It is a quotient, not an extension.** Adjoining the electromagnetic coordinates to Λ₉ as new axes
3588:  gives **E = 3,900** against E(Λ₉) = 0 — Theorem 17.1 in the direction that matters, since every one
3589:  of them is a function of coordinates Λ already carries. **A derived coordinate cannot improve
3590:  closure either.**
3591: 
3592:  **And it is not composability.** §12.11.0's transit condition 2S′ ≤ g admits 1,169 cells; the
3593:  electromagnetic condition and the composability condition share **0.0004 bits of a possible 0.633**.
3594:  The first is about state succession — whether a target is a legal source. The second is about
3595:  whether a photon connects them. **They are near-independent predicates on the same cells, and the
3596:  book has been calling the first one a transition.** Registers 442–444.
3597: 
3598:  **And the same trade, measured across four schemes rather than two.** The tower as built uses jK. The
3599:  other three standard schemes — LS, LK and jj — were rebuilt from their recoupling chains, and two
3600:  reproduce their stated Λ₁₃ counts exactly from the chain alone: **jK 199,130 and LK 341,150.** LS and
3601:  jj depend on a looseness convention that is named and not printed, and two committed readings of it
3602:  **bracket** the stated figures rather than determining them: LS ∈ [383,065, 597,325] ∋ 431,050 and
3603:  jj ∈ [160,380, 244,060] ∋ 206,520.
3604: 
3605:  **The chains are standard.** NIST states LK as *the core's orbital momentum coupled with the external
3606:  electron's to give L, then L coupled with the spin of the core to obtain K*, and jK as
3607:  ℓ₁+s₁ = j₁, j₁+ℓ₂ = K, K+s₂ = J. Cowan and Andrew, *JOSA* **55**, 502 (1965), treat exactly these
3608:  four as the four types of pure coupling for two-electron configurations — a precedent for the set,
3609:  not only for the members.
3610: 
3611:     **The exact J multiset is identical in all four schemes, in every configuration tested.**
3612: 
3613:  Verified across fifteen configurations by computing the multiset through the jK chain, the LS chain
3614:  and the jj chain independently. A coupling scheme is a basis change; the atoms do not move. **So the
3615:  four cell counts, spanning a factor of 2.17, price four ROUTES to one object.** §12.11.4's sentence
3616:  one level down says it already — *the exact J-set is the same whether J is reached through K or
3617:  directly, 12 of 12; the envelopes differ, 64.4% against 39.4%. The index remembers the route; the
3618:  atom does not.* Register 433.
3619: 
3620:  The privileged route exists because the outer electron's spin is ½: the final triangle degenerates to
3621:  the mutual bound |2J − 2K| ≤ 1, which is admissible on both sides and closed, losing only the
3622:  parity point 2J = 2K. The smallest quantum of angular momentum is the largest the constraint
3623:  language can hold exactly. And the route the language prefers is jK coupling — the scheme the
3624:  atoms of Part V actually realise at high n, and for the same structural reason: the weak coupling
3625:  goes last. [Interpretation, not theorem.]
3626: 
","stderr":""}

content.text:
{"returncode":0,"stdout":"14681: ### Three excluded forms
14682: 
14683: **Two constraint forms were already excluded — sums and differences (§17.2) — and the tower requires a third: symmetric bounds. Every coupling axis's exact ceiling is symmetric under particle-hole conjugation, terms(ℓᵏ) = terms(ℓ^{4ℓ+2−k}), verified exactly for every k on the p and d shells, and a symmetric non-constant function is not monotone, so the admissibility condition (§14.4) cannot carry it: min(g, 4f+2−g) for spin, the conjugation ceiling for seniority, and max2J(ℓ, k) — unimodal, peaking at half filling, 25 at f⁷ and zero at closure — for the core's J. One reflection, three appearances. The envelope gap decomposes into three distinct parts, and at the caps of §7.4 the ninth axis's gap is parity 5, fold 1, both 1 while the eleventh's is ceiling 16, parity 24, triangle 17 — three machines, the reflection (conjugation), the congruence (fermion parity), and the triangle (coupling additivity, one sum and one difference, precisely §17.2's two exclusions wearing physics), and no coupling axis escapes all three. Behind them is one law, three instances deep before the triangle made it four: every coupling coordinate's exact physical bound requires either two parents or a congruence, and the tree carries only one — spin needing min(g, 4f+2−g), seniority the conjugation ceiling, the core's J a non-monotone envelope. Each admissible extension is the monotone envelope of its physics. One half of the triangle survives the four-cap check: the region {|2L−2S| ≤ 2J ≤ 2L+2S} is join-closed — zero failures at caps 6, 8, 10 and 12 — and meet-broken at every one, by 2,862, 12,489, 40,887 and 110,229 failing meets, so certainty survives upward and dies downward, which is the reflection asymmetry (§8.4) stated as an inequality. And the check sharpens the statement: impose the parity congruence as well and the join closure dies too — 1,848 failures at cap 6 — so the surviving half belongs to the parity-free triangle and to nothing larger. Three bodies carry all three excluded forms at once; §36.3 runs the method on that case and finds the maximal forbidden case is the solved one.**
14684: 
14685: *the three symmetric ceilings under particle-hole conjugation, verified for every k on the p and d shells; the join-closure and meet-failure counts of the surviving half-triangle {|2L−2S| ≤ 2J ≤ 2L+2S} over unordered pairs at box caps 6, 8, 10, 12; the parity-congruence collapse measured at cap 6.*
14686: 
14687: Proved — M §12.11.2; Pauli 1925; Racah 1942; Wigner 1927; Dilworth 1940.
14688: 
14689: > **Prior art: the equivalence of a shell's terms under particle-hole conjugation is the complementarity of Pauli (1925) developed by Racah, *Phys. Rev.* 61 (1942); the triangle condition |L−S| ≤ J ≤ L+S on vector coupling is Wigner, *Gruppentheorie* (1927); that a set closed under one lattice operation need not be closed under the other — join without meet — is elementary lattice theory after Dilworth (1940). That these three symmetric forms are exactly what excludes the coupling ceilings from a monotone presentation, that the envelope gap decomposes into reflection, congruence and triangle with no coupling axis escaping all three, and that the surviving half-triangle is join-closed and meet-broken by 2,862, 12,489, 40,887 and 110,229 — dying at the join too once parity is imposed, at 1,848 — is this book's.**
14690: 
14691: ### Law versus extent, and what E measures
14692: 
14693: **Counting coordinates close exactly; coupling coordinates close as envelopes; there is no third kind in this object. The origins table (§7.1) has four rows — Pauli, the hydrogenic solution and counting give single-coordinate exact bounds, which is why E(Λ) = 0 was available at all, while vector coupling gives envelopes provably and permanently, because its exact form is made of the three excluded shapes (§12.11.2). The sharper statement is about where each axis's bound is taken from, the same distinction between a deduction and a fit that §22 draws for brackets. Reading the thirteen bounds by provenance gives three values, not two: the first ten are taken from a law that exists independently of Λ — the hydrogenic radial solution, Pauli, counting, vector coupling on each end, Racah's seniority — while the eleventh, 2J_c ≤ φ̂(k), is taken from the extent of Λ itself. For φ̂ is not derived but observed: computed at the caps of §7.4 it is {1: 3, 2: 4, 3: 5}, and the largest 2J_c the set actually realises at each occupancy is {1: 3, 2: 4, 3: 5} — the same numbers, because φ̂ is the envelope of the set's own extent. A bound taken from the law closes exactly; a bound taken from the extent closes only to an envelope. That is why exactness is lost at the eleventh axis and not before it. === §17.3 body ===
### 17.3 E3 — which constraints may be imposed
 This one took three wrong statements to reach, which is recorded in Chapter 28. The criterion is:

 **And for a constraint on a DIFFERENCE the criterion is convexity, which is proved here.**

    **The interval property.** For δ = f − ℓ on a sublattice of a product of chains and any
    cells a, b:  min(δa, δb) ≤ δ(a ∨ b) ≤ max(δa, δb), and the same for a ∧ b.

 *Proof.* δ(a∨b) = max(f_a,f_b) − max(ℓ_a,ℓ_b). Take f_a ≥ f_b. If ℓ_a ≥ ℓ_b then δ(a∨b) = δa.
 Otherwise δ(a∨b) = f_a − ℓ_b ≥ f_b − ℓ_b = δb and δ(a∨b) ≤ f_a − ℓ_a = δa. Either way it lies
 between. The meet is dual. ∎ **Verified with zero violations on all 1,367,031 pairs of Λ₉**, for
 δ = f − ℓ and for σ = 2S′ − 2S.

    **Criterion.** δ⁻¹(T) is a sublattice of Λ **iff T ∩ range(δ) is convex in range(δ)**.

 **How much of the family this supplies, measured.** Every convex preimage is closed — the criterion
 is sound in the direction it is used. **It is nowhere near complete**: on the three ambients of
 §14.5 the convex preimages are **8.2%, 10.3% and 0.8%** of all closed subsets. So the criterion
 decides the constraints this book actually imposes and does not enumerate the closed sets. **A
 sufficient condition tested for necessity and found to be a small part of what it describes**, which
 is what §4.6 asks of any criterion before it is relied on.

    **Scope: Λ must be closed.** The criterion is a statement about subsets of a
    CLOSED ambient, and it fails where the ambient is not one.

 **Tested on the periodic table, which is the case that shows it.** The eighteen-column table is
 **not a sublattice** — its own joins and meets leave it — and there the criterion misses and a band
 fails at E = 5. Janet's table **is** a sublattice, and there the criterion is 4 of 4 and the same
 band closes at E = 0. The condition is not decoration: **the one object in this book whose answer is
 independently known is also the one that violates the criterion's hypothesis**, and it does so
 because E(table) = 36 is exactly the statement that it is not closed. Register 449.

 Verified at two cap settings, 36 of 36, including every case where the wider values become
 attainable and a set convex only by accident of the range flips to failing.

 **A difference is not a lattice homomorphism** — §18.2 refuses ν = e − δ as an axis for exactly that
 reason — **but it is an interval map**, which is weaker than a homomorphism and stronger than
 nothing: the image of a join is not determined, it is bracketed. **And convexity is what closure
 means for a quantity that is only bracketed.** A convex set is one a bracket cannot escape.

 **This gives §12.11.2's second excluded form a criterion it did not have.** A congruence is excluded
 exactly when the set it defines has a hole in the attained range — and the hole's POSITION is what
 matters, not the modulus, because a reparametrisation that moves the hole to an endpoint restores
 closure. Seniority parity at axis 10, the conjugation ceiling at axis 12, and the electromagnetic
 parity rule are three instances of one criterion rather than three separate refusals. Register 440.

    { h ≤ q } is closed ⟺ h(x∨y) ≤ q for all x, y with h(x), h(y) ≤ q

 **100% over 2,513 tests, nine functions.**

 **The essential feature is that it is *q*-dependent.** Admissibility belongs to the *pair* (*h*, *q*), not to *h* alone — which is why *a* + *b* ≤ 3 can be closed where *a* + *b* ≤ 4 is not, and why every *q*-free criterion attempted before this one failed.

 **Meet never breaks it.** For monotone *h* with *h*(*x*), *h*(*y*) ≤ *q*, *x*∧*y* ≤ *x* gives *h*(*x*∧*y*) ≤ *q* at once. **Only the join can break it**, and it does so when the join raises *h* above both arguments.

    Sums and products fail because a join raises every coordinate at once, and anything
    accumulating across coordinates accumulates the raises.

 **Λ's seven constraints are all safe by inspection**: each reads one coordinate, or a minimum of two. **None sums.** That is why Λ is closed and the periodic table is not — and it is checkable without touching a cell.

cd /home/claude/gate && cat >> em36.py <<'EOF'

def closed_np(cells):
    """Vectorised closedness under join and meet for a set of integer tuples. Returns (n, join_fail, meet_fail)."""
    import numpy as np
    A = np.array(cells, dtype=np.int64)
    base = A.max(axis=0) + 1
    w = np.cumprod(np.concatenate(([1], base[:-1])))
    keys = A @ w
    keyset = np.sort(keys)
    jf = mf = 0
    for i in range(len(A)):
        kj = np.maximum(A[i], A) @ w
        km = np.minimum(A[i], A) @ w
        jf += int((~np.isin(kj, keyset, assume_unique=False)).sum())
        mf += int((~np.isin(km, keyset, assume_unique=False)).sum())
    return len(A), jf, mf
EOF
python3 - <<'EOF' 2>&1 | tee em36-D.txt
import sys; sys.path.insert(0,'.')

for caps,exp in [((3,3,1,3,1),1654),((3,3,2,3,2),2664),((4,4,2,6,2),44153),((4,4,3,6,3),60164)]:

    print(f'caps {caps} |Λ9|={len(L9)} spin-rule cells={n} join-fail={jf} meet-fail={mf} -> E=0: {jf==0 and mf==0}')
EOF

# em37.py — verification instrument for OWED row 37 (§12.11.8 quotient-not-extension; MI near-independence)
import sys, math
import numpy as np
sys.path.insert(0, '.')
from em36 import L9c, dl, ds, multipole

MP = {'M1': 0, 'E1': 1, 'E2': 2, 'E3': 3}

def closure_np(cells):
    """Iterative join/meet closure to a fixed point in the product of integer chains (vectorised).
    Returns (closure_size, rounds)."""
    A = np.array(cells, dtype=np.int64)
    off = A.min(axis=0); A = A - off                     # shift to non-negative for keying
    rounds = 0
    while True:
        rounds += 1
        base = A.max(axis=0) + 1
        w = np.cumprod(np.concatenate(([1], base[:-1])))
        keys = A @ w
        keyset = np.unique(keys)
        new_rows = []
        for i in range(len(A)):
            J = np.maximum(A[i], A); M = np.minimum(A[i], A)
            kj = J @ w; km = M @ w
            nj = ~np.isin(kj, keyset); nm = ~np.isin(km, keyset)
            if nj.any(): new_rows.append(J[nj])
            if nm.any(): new_rows.append(M[nm])
        if not new_rows:
            return len(A), rounds
        N = np.unique(np.vstack(new_rows), axis=0)
        A = np.unique(np.vstack([A, N]), axis=0)

def H(p):
    return 0.0 if p in (0, 1) else -(p*math.log2(p) + (1-p)*math.log2(1-p))

def MI(a, b):
    n = len(a); c = {}
    for x, y in zip(a, b): c[(x, y)] = c.get((x, y), 0) + 1
    pa = sum(a)/n; pb = sum(b)/n
    mi = 0.0
    for (x, y), k in c.items():
        pxy = k/n; px = pa if x else 1-pa; py = pb if y else 1-pb
        mi += pxy*math.log2(pxy/(px*py))
    return mi

if __name__ == '__main__':
    part = sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else 'A'
    L9 = L9c()
    if part == 'A':
        cands = {
            'δ (signed Δℓ)':            lambda c: (dl(c),),
            'σ (signed ΔS)':            lambda c: (ds(c),),
            'δ, σ (signed)':            lambda c: (dl(c), ds(c)),
            '|δ|, |σ|':                 lambda c: (abs(dl(c)), abs(ds(c))),
            'δ, σ, multipole':          lambda c: (dl(c), ds(c), MP[multipole(c)]),
            '|δ|, |σ|, multipole':      lambda c: (abs(dl(c)), abs(ds(c)), MP[multipole(c)]),
            'multipole only':           lambda c: (MP[multipole(c)],),
            '|σ| only':                 lambda c: (abs(ds(c)),),
            'δ, |σ|':                   lambda c: (dl(c), abs(ds(c))),
            '|δ|, σ':                   lambda c: (abs(dl(c)), ds(c)),
        }
        for name, h in cands.items():
            S = [c + h(c) for c in L9]
            n, r = closure_np(S)
            print(f'adjoin {name:24s}: |Λ9′| = {len(S)}  closure = {n}  E = {n-len(S)}  rounds {r}')
    elif part == 'B':
        comp = [1 if c[6] >= 1 else 0 for c in L9]
        preds = {
            'E1 ∧ ΔS=0 (LS-allowed dipole)': lambda c: multipole(c) == 'E1' and ds(c) == 0,
            'E1 (|Δℓ|=1)':                   lambda c: multipole(c) == 'E1',
            'ΔS=0':                          lambda c: ds(c) == 0,
            'E1 ∧ ΔS≠0 (intercombination)':  lambda c: multipole(c) == 'E1' and ds(c) != 0,
            'M1 ∧ ΔS=0':                     lambda c: multipole(c) == 'M1' and ds(c) == 0,
        }
        print(f'composable: {sum(comp)} cells, H = {H(sum(comp)/len(L9)):.4f} bits')
        for name, p in preds.items():
            a = [1 if p(c) else 0 for c in L9]
            print(f'{name:32s} cells {sum(a):4d}  H = {H(sum(a)/len(L9)):.4f}  MI(with composable) = {MI(a, comp):.6f} bits')

{"returncode":0,"stdout":"### 14.1 The characterisation
 Theorem 14.1 (A.2). X is closed iff X = ℛ(X), where ℛ reconstructs value sets and pairwise monotone
 bounds from X's own extension.

 **This is not new mathematics and the book gains by saying so.** A.2 is **Bergman's Double-projection
 Theorem** specialised to products of chains — a sublattice of a finite product of lattices is
 determined by its two-fold projections — itself a consequence of **Baker and Pixley (1975)** for any
 algebra with a majority term, of which the lattice median is one. Λ's coordinates are counts, so each
 factor is a chain, and a sublattice of a product of two chains is exactly a staircase cut by monotone
 bounds, which is what ℛ recovers as φ_ij. The proof in §16.1 is correct and fifty years late.

 **And there are two further owners, both located after this chapter was written.** The property
 E(X) = 0 is *global consistency* of a binary constraint network, and the certificates are
 **Montanari 1974** — for monotone constraints, path consistency implies global consistency — and
 **Dechter 1992**, *From local to global consistency*, which gives decomposability at strong
 (w\*+1)-consistency on induced width w\*. **Freuder 1982 is a different theorem and this book has
 been citing it for Dechter's**: Freuder gives *backtrack-free search* on a graph of width w under
 strong (w+1)-consistency, and says explicitly that even width 2 demands strong 3-consistency. The
 mis-citation is corrected here and recorded at register 400.

 **And the constraint class has a name.** A binary constraint that is (α, β)-monotone with
 α, β ∈ {≤, ≥} is a **staircase** constraint, and the connected row-convex class containing it is
 closed under composition, intersection and transposition — **Deville, Barták and Van Hentenryck,
 *Artificial Intelligence* 1999**. φ̂ recovers exactly a staircase, so the operator of §6.1 has been
 building a named object since Chapter 6. Register 401.

 **What follows is that E(Λ) = 0 is the discovery that Λ is a sublattice**, and sublattices have been
 binary-determined since 1975. The development is at A.2; the register carries the finding at 224.

def dp_relaxation_size(cells):
    """Double-projection relaxation: {x ∈ ∏ V_i : (x_i, x_j) ∈ π_ij(X) for all i<j}. Returns its size."""
    import itertools
    cells = list(set(cells)); d = len(cells[0])
    V = [sorted(set(c[i] for c in cells)) for i in range(d)]
    P = {}
    for i in range(d):
        for j in range(i+1, d):
            P[(i, j)] = set((c[i], c[j]) for c in cells)
    # backtracking enumeration with pairwise pruning
    count = 0
    def rec(prefix):
        nonlocal count
        k = len(prefix)
        if k == d: count += 1; return
        for v in V[k]:
            if all((prefix[i], v) in P[(i, k)] for i in range(k)):
                rec(prefix + (v,))
    rec(())
    return count
EOF

 3595|  whether a photon connects them. **They are near-independent predicates on the same cells, and the
 3596|  book has been calling the first one a transition.** Registers 442–444.

 3598|  **And the same trade, measured across four schemes rather than two.** The tower as built uses jK. The
 3599|  other three standard schemes — LS, LK and jj — were rebuilt from their recoupling chains, and two
 3600|  reproduce their stated Λ₁₃ counts exactly from the chain alone: **jK 199,130 and LK 341,150.** LS and

 3602|  **bracket** the stated figures rather than determining them: LS ∈ [383,065, 597,325] ∋ 431,050 and

 3611|     **The exact J multiset is identical in all four schemes, in every configuration tested.**

 3615|  four cell counts, spanning a factor of 2.17, price four ROUTES to one object.** §12.11.4's sentence
 3616|  one level down says it already — *the exact J-set is the same whether J is reached through K or
 3617|  directly, 12 of 12; the envelopes differ, 64.4% against 39.4%. The index remembers the route; the
 3618|  atom does not.* Register 433.
 3619| 
 3620|  The privileged route exists because the outer electron's spin is ½: the final triangle degenerates to
 3621|  the mutual bound |2J − 2K| ≤ 1, which is admissible on both sides and closed, losing only the
 3622|  parity point 2J = 2K. The smallest quantum of angular momentum is the largest the constraint
 3623|  language can hold exactly. And the route the language prefers is jK coupling — the scheme the
 3624|  atoms of Part V actually realise at high n, and for the same structural reason: the weak coupling
 3625|  goes last. [Interpretation, not theorem.]

 3629|  the nucleon index, and the string partition function, and the Kreuzer–Skarke frontier, and Appendix D's

 3631|  the index, close it, read E(X), record every failure.
 3632|

 3634|  the process; Part I indexes the rules; Appendix D indexes the mathematics and closes it at E
 3635|  = 0. A book whose method is applied to its own contents four times over is a method with a
 3636|  demonstration, not a demonstration with a method.
 3637| 
 3638|       The method is the book, and the book is the method. The cylinder is the case that proved
 3639|       it could be done and the case that showed what it costs.
 3640|

 3642|  Λ is fibred over q, the number of electrons transferred. Not over any property of a single
 3643|  configuration — over the movement between two.
 3644| 
 3645|       One end is a parent (n, ℓ, k) with its spin 2S. The other is a target (e, f) with its occupancy g. They
 3646|       meet at q.
 3647| 
 3648|  **Chapter 7 introduces both ends and never says the pair is the object.** The shape says it: |Λ| = Σ_q |A_q| · |B_q|, and there is no factorisation that does not pass through the transfer.
 3649| 
 3650| ### 13.3 Which is why "index of transitions"
 3651|  An index of states would fibre over a state variable. This one fibres over a difference, and every
 3652|  structural result follows from that:
 3653| 
 3654|   finding                               where it comes from
 3655| 
 3656|   the fibres are two-body products      the two ends of the tree
 3657| 
 3658|   \                                     A_q\                                 falls as   B   ris   the transfer is conserved between
 3659|                                                                              \          _   es    them
 3660|                                                                                         q
 3661|                                                                                         \
 3662| 
 3663|   g ≤ q is the most active constraint   it is the coupling itself
 3664| 
 3665|   rank is modular                       the transfer redistributes without
 3666|                                         loss
 3667| 
 3668| ### 13.4 And what the cylinder does not carry
 3669|  The lattice supplies kinematics and no dynamics. What configurations exist, which transitions are
 3670|  admissible, what is conserved — all structural. Which transition actually occurs is not.
 3671| 
 3672|     1,113,045,672 maximal chains satisfy every constraint in this book (§12.9). The Aufbau ordering
 3673|     is one of them. Structure does not choose; energy does, and energy enters only through Chapter
 3674|     17's measured levels.
 3675| 
 3676|  **That is the sharpest statement of what the index can and cannot do**, and it is a statement about its shape: **a phase space with the Hamiltonian removed can bound and refuse, and cannot predict.**
 3677| 
 3678| # PART III — THE LAW
 3679| 
 3680| ## 14. Closure
 3681|  A set is closed when nothing its own structure admits is missing from it.
 3682| 
 3683| ### 14.1 The characterisation
 3684|  Theorem 14.1 (A.2). X is closed iff X = ℛ(X), where ℛ reconstructs value sets and pairwise monotone
 3685|  bounds from X's own extension.
 3686| 
 3687|  **This is not new mathematics and the book gains by saying so.** A.2 is **Bergman's Double-projection
 3688|  Theorem** specialised to products of chains — a sublattice of a finite product of lattices is
 3689|  determined by its two-fold projections — itself a consequence of **Baker and Pixley (1975)** for any
 3690|  algebra with a majority term, of which the lattice median is one. Λ's coordinates are counts, so each
 3691|  factor is a chain, and a sublattice of a product of two chains is exactly a staircase cut by monotone
 3692|  bounds, which is what ℛ recovers as φ_ij. The proof in §16.1 is correct and fifty years late.
 3693| 
 3694|  **And there are two further owners, both located after this chapter was written.** The property
 3695|  E(X) = 0 is *global consistency* of a binary constraint network, and the certificates are
 3696|  **Montanari 1974** — for monotone constraints, path consistency implies global consistency — and
 3697|  **Dechter 1992**, *From local to global consistency*, which gives decomposability at strong
 3698|  (w\*+1)-consistency on induced width w\*. **Freuder 1982 is a different theorem and this book has
 3699|  been citing it for Dechter's**: Freuder gives *backtrack-free search* on a graph of width w under
 3700|  strong (w+1)-consistency, and says explicitly that even width 2 demands strong 3-consistency. The
 3701|  mis-citation is corrected here and recorded at register 400.
 3702| 
 3703|  **And the constraint class has a name.** A binary constraint that is (α, β)-monotone with
 3704|  α, β ∈ {≤, ≥} is a **staircase** constraint, and the connected row-convex class containing it is
 3705|  closed under composition, intersection and transposition — **Deville, Barták and Van Hentenryck,
 3706|  *Artificial Intelligence* 1999**. φ̂ recovers exactly a staircase, so the operator of §6.1 has been
 3707|  building a named object since Chapter 6. Register 401.
 3708| 
 3709|  **What follows is that E(Λ) = 0 is the discovery that Λ is a sublattice**, and sublattices have been
 3710|  binary-determined since 1975. The development is at A.2; the register carries the finding at 224.
 3711| 
 3712| ### 14.2 R is a closure operator
 3713|  Extensive, monotone, idempotent — 150 of 150 on all three axioms.
 3714| 
 3715|  So E(X) = |ℛ(X)| − |X| is a closure defect, a standard object in Galois theory, formal concept analysis
 3716|  and database dependency theory.
 3717| 
 3718|  **This book claims no novelty for the machinery.** What is offered is the application: computing the closure defect of an *index*, and finding that the periodic table's is 36 while Λ's is 0.
 3719| 
 3720| ### 14.3 The scope, stated exactly
 3721|  Theorem 14.1 requires each coordinate to be presented as a chain. That is not the same as requiring the
 3722|  factors to be chains: any distributive factor can be so presented, by Birkhoff, as the down-sets of its
 3723|  join-irreducibles — one chain per irreducible.
 3724| 
 3725|  What fails is bundling. ℛ reconstructs coordinate by coordinate, so folding two chains into one
 3726|  non-chain coordinate hides structure from it. In tests, the same sets presented bundled and presented
 3727|  decomposed both gave 80/80 agreement — the theorem survives, but only when the presentation
 3728|  respects it.
 3729| 
 3730| ### 14.4 The three consequences
 3731|  Closure yields three properties, developed in the next three chapters:
 3732| 
 3733| ### 14.5 The family of all closed sets
 3734| 
 3735|  A closed index is one object. **The closed subsets of a closed index are a family**, and this book
 3736|  has carried the question of what that family is since Λ was built. It is answerable by enumeration
 3737|  at small size, and the answer is standard once it is seen.
 3738| 
 3739|   ambient        cells   closed subsets   of 2ⁿ    ∩ closed   ∪ closed
 3740|   2 × 2 × 2          8       **73**       28.5%     **100%**     64.4%
 3741|   3 × 3              9      **146**       28.5%     **100%**     68.3%
 3742|   2 × 2 × 2 × 2     16      **731**        1.1%     **100%**     32.6%
 3743| 
 3744|     **The closed sets of ℛ form a MOORE FAMILY: closed under intersection, containing
 3745|     the whole index, and NOT closed under union.**
 3746| 
 3747|  That is the standard fact about any closure operator — the closed sets of a closure operator are a
 3748|  Moore family, and the correspondence between operators, families and lattices is cryptomorphic. **It
 3749|  is worth stating here because the asymmetry is ℛ's own, one level up.** ℛ carries meets and refuses
 3750|  joins in §14.2; its family of fixed points does the same, at 100% against 32–68%.
 3751| 
 3752|  **And it is the setting in which register 458's finding lives.** Λ₉ is closed and 300 of 300 random
 3753|  subsets of it are open, because the closed ones are a Moore family inside a power set — a vanishing
 3754|  minority, and the only place from which the open ones can be measured.
 3755| 
 3756|  **The count for Λ itself is open.** Brute force is 2⁹⁷⁶. The Moore-family structure gives the route,
 3757|  since a Moore family is determined by its meet-irreducible members, and §8.4 already counts those
 3758|  for Λ under a different name. Q item R. Register 461.
 3759| 
 3760|  **And the FAMILY is examined at §14.6**, where it is shown to be open — every member closed,
 3761|  the family not — which is why counting it for Λ is a question about an object that cannot be stated
 3762|  rather than one that is merely large.
 3763|

"""
Batch 7 EM-index verification (MC-36/37/38/39).
Verified-before-written: every figure recomputed on the rebuilt tower.

Coordinate order:
 Λ8:  n0 l1 k2 q3 e4 f5 g6 2S7
 Λ9:  + 2S'8
 ...  + v9 2Jc10 2K11 2J12
"""
from itertools import product as iproduct
from math import log2
import tower  # the validated instrument

# ---------- closure operator R (iterative join/meet sublattice closure) ----------
def R_closure(cells):
    """Iterative sublattice closure: close under componentwise meet(min) and join(max)
    to a fixpoint. This is the ℛ the record uses (MC-31 note: for non-tree sets the
    single double-projection pass can differ; iterate to fixpoint)."""
    S = set(cells)
    if not S:
        return S
    changed = True
    while changed:
        changed = False
        cur = list(S)
        new = set()
        for i in range(len(cur)):
            a = cur[i]
            for j in range(i, len(cur)):
                b = cur[j]
                mn = tuple(min(x,y) for x,y in zip(a,b))
                mx = tuple(max(x,y) for x,y in zip(a,b))
                if mn not in S: new.add(mn)
                if mx not in S: new.add(mx)
        if new:
            S |= new
            changed = True
    return S

def E(cells):
    s=set(cells)
    return len(R_closure(s)) - len(s)

# ---------- sanity: E(Λ_d)=0 at every stage (double check instrument+closure) ----------
def check_stage_closure():
    out={}
    for d in [8,9,10]:  # 8,9,10 are cheap; 11+ are large for O(n^2) closure
        cells=tower.STAGES[d]()
        out[d]=E(cells)
    return out

# ---------- EM maps ----------
# Δℓ = f - l  (target subshell f=index5, source l=index1), defined at Λ8
# ΔS = 2S' - 2S (2S'=index8, 2S=index7), defined at Λ9
def dl(c):  return c[5]-c[1]
def dS(c):  return c[8]-c[7]

# multipole from (Δℓ, parity): Δℓ=0→M1, 1→E1, 2→E2, 3→E3 (lowest whose parity matches)
# parity of the transition = parity of Δℓ; E-type when Δℓ odd, M1 when Δℓ even (for the low orders here)
def multipole(c):
    d=abs(dl(c))
    return {0:'M1',1:'E1',2:'E2',3:'E3'}.get(d, f'>{d}')

if __name__=='__main__':
    print('stage closure E (expect 0):', check_stage_closure())

    L9=tower.L9()
    print('|Λ9| =', len(L9))

    # ---- image rectangle: (multipole, ΔS) ----
    from collections import Counter
    img=Counter()
    for c in L9:
        img[(multipole(c), dS(c))]+=1
    # print E1 and M1 rows across ΔS=0..3
    print('\\nimage (multipole, ΔS):')
    for mp in ['E1','M1','E2','E3']:
        row=[img.get((mp,s),0) for s in range(0,4)]
        if any(row): print(f'  {mp}:', row)
    # E1 cells with ΔS != 0 (intercombination count)
    e1_inter=sum(v for (mp,s),v in img.items() if mp=='E1' and s!=0)
    print('E1 with ΔS!=0 (intercombination):', e1_inter)

    # image cell count + E of the image
    image_cells=set((({'M1':0,'E1':1,'E2':2,'E3':3}[multipole(c)]), dS(c)) for c in L9)
    print('image distinct cells:', len(image_cells), '| E(image)=', E(image_cells))

    # ---- spin imposition σ^{-1}({0}) : keep cells with ΔS=0 ----
    spin0=[c for c in L9 if dS(c)==0]
    print('\\nspin σ^{-1}({0}) on Λ9: kept', len(spin0), '| E=', E(spin0))

    # ---- parity imposition on Λ8: δ^{-1}({-1,+1}) : keep |Δℓ|=1 ----
    L8=tower.L8()
    par=[c for c in L8 if dl(c) in (-1,1)]
    print('parity δ^{-1}({-1,+1}) on Λ8: kept', len(par), '| E=', E(par))

import numpy as np

def _unique_rows(A):
    # A: (n,d) int array -> unique rows
    A = np.ascontiguousarray(A)
    v = A.view([('', A.dtype)] * A.shape[1])
    _, idx = np.unique(v, return_index=True)
    return A[np.sort(idx)]

def R_closure_np(cells):
    A = _unique_rows(np.array(sorted(set(cells)), dtype=np.int16))
    while True:
        n = A.shape[0]
        # all pairwise via broadcasting: (n,1,d) vs (1,n,d)
        P = A[:,None,:]; Q = A[None,:,:]
        mn = np.minimum(P,Q).reshape(-1, A.shape[1])
        mx = np.maximum(P,Q).reshape(-1, A.shape[1])
        cand = np.vstack([A, mn, mx])
        U = _unique_rows(cand)
        if U.shape[0] == n:
            return U
        A = U

def E_np(cells):
    s = set(map(tuple, cells))
    U = R_closure_np(s)
    return U.shape[0] - len(s)

def _uniq(A):
    A=np.ascontiguousarray(A.astype(np.int16))
    v=A.view([('',A.dtype)]*A.shape[1])
    _,idx=np.unique(v,return_index=True)
    return A[np.sort(idx)]

def R_closure_chunk(cells, block=256):
    A=_uniq(np.array(sorted(set(cells)),dtype=np.int16))
    while True:
        n=A.shape[0]; d=A.shape[1]
        pieces=[A]
        for s in range(0,n,block):
            blk=A[s:s+block]                     # (b,d)
            mn=np.minimum(blk[:,None,:],A[None,:,:]).reshape(-1,d)
            mx=np.maximum(blk[:,None,:],A[None,:,:]).reshape(-1,d)
            pieces.append(_uniq(np.vstack([mn,mx])))
        U=_uniq(np.vstack(pieces))
        if U.shape[0]==n:
            return U

# Sub-pass segmentation: one CALL processes a bounded range of source-blocks
# against the full current set A, appending new min/max rows to a growth buffer.
# When a pass's blocks are exhausted, fold buffer into A and start next pass.
import numpy as np, json, os, time, sys

def _uniq(A):
    A=np.ascontiguousarray(A.astype(np.int32))
    v=A.view([('',A.dtype)]*A.shape[1])
    _,idx=np.unique(v,return_index=True)
    return A[np.sort(idx)]

def process(state, nblocks, block=64, budget=200.0):
    A=np.load(state+'.npy')
    meta=json.load(open(state+'.json'))
    if meta.get('done'):
        print('done: n=',meta['n'],'iter',meta['iter']); return
    n,d=A.shape
    cursor=meta.get('cursor',0)
    # growth buffer file
    gb=state+'_grow.npy'
    grow = np.load(gb) if os.path.exists(gb) else np.zeros((0,d),dtype=np.int32)
    t=time.time(); did=0
    while cursor<n and did<nblocks and (time.time()-t)<budget:
        blk=A[cursor:cursor+block]
        mn=np.minimum(blk[:,None,:],A[None,:,:]).reshape(-1,d)
        mx=np.maximum(blk[:,None,:],A[None,:,:]).reshape(-1,d)
        u=_uniq(np.vstack([mn,mx]))
        grow=_uniq(np.vstack([grow,u]))
        cursor+=block; did+=1
    if cursor>=n:
        # pass complete: fold grow into A
        U=_uniq(np.vstack([A,grow]))
        meta['iter']+=1; meta['last_add']=int(U.shape[0]-n); meta['n']=int(U.shape[0])
        meta['cursor']=0
        if U.shape[0]==n: meta['done']=True
        np.save(state+'.npy', U)
        if os.path.exists(gb): os.remove(gb)
        json.dump(meta, open(state+'.json','w'))
        print(f"PASS {meta['iter']} complete: n {n}->{U.shape[0]} (+{U.shape[0]-n}) done={meta.get('done',False)} [{time.time()-t:.0f}s]")
    else:
        np.save(gb, grow)
        meta['cursor']=cursor
        json.dump(meta, open(state+'.json','w'))
        print(f"pass {meta['iter']+1} partial: cursor {cursor}/{n}, grow={grow.shape[0]} [{time.time()-t:.0f}s]")

if __name__=='__main__':
    state=sys.argv[1]; nblocks=int(sys.argv[2])

import numpy as np, itertools

### Which selection rules a closed index will accept

**A cell of Λ is an electromagnetic transition, and the rules that decide whether a photon connects two configurations — multipole, parity, the change in spin — are not coordinates of Λ but functions of the coordinates it already carries. So the question is not what they are but whether the index will hold them: a selection rule presented as a set of admissible cells may be imposed on Λ₉ with closure surviving exactly when that set is convex in the range of the quantity defining it, which is §17.3's criterion arriving where it can be measured. The spin rule ΔS = 0 is the diagonal of a difference, σ⁻¹({0}), and a diagonal is two monotone one-parent bounds at once; it is convex in range, and imposing it keeps 526 of Λ₉'s 1,654 cells at defect zero, holding not at one cap but at four settings of §7.4 — 1,654, 2,664, 44,153 and 60,164 cells, E = 0 at each. The parity rule |Δℓ| = 1 is δ⁻¹({−1, +1}), and here the set has a hole: it admits Δℓ = −1 and Δℓ = +1 and refuses the Δℓ = 0 between them, so it is not convex in range, and imposing it keeps 840 cells at a defect of 750 — the closure of the punctured set fills the hole straight back in. The two rules divide on exactly the property the criterion names, and the criterion says which in advance rather than after the count. The parity rule is the fourth instance of §12.11.2's second excluded form — a bound that is a symmetric window rather than a one-sided cap — and it is the first for which the criterion also names the repair that would work: any reparametrisation that moves the hole to an endpoint of the range makes the set convex and closes it, at the cost of no longer being the parity rule. Half the missing electromagnetic law can be imposed on the index and half cannot, and the line between the halves is not physical but order-theoretic: a rule is admissible when its image is an interval, and refused when its image is an interval with a point removed.**

*the spin rule σ⁻¹({0}) imposed on Λ₉, 526 cells at E = 0 and stable across the four caps 1,654 / 2,664 / 44,153 / 60,164 (the four-cap sizes carried from the record); the parity rule δ⁻¹({−1, +1}) imposed on Λ₉, 840 cells at E = 750; convexity-in-range read on Δℓ = f − ℓ and ΔS = 2S′ − 2S, at the caps of §7.4, (n, e, ℓ, k, f) = (3, 3, 1, 3, 1).*

Proved — M §12.11.8, §17.3; Russell & Saunders 1925; Laporte 1924; Wigner 1927.

> **Prior art: that the electric-dipole spin rule is ΔS = 0 in LS coupling is Russell & Saunders, Astrophys. J. 61 (1925) 38, and that the parity rule is |Δℓ| = 1 is Laporte, Z. Phys. 23 (1924) 135, its group-theoretic ground Wigner, Z. Phys. 43 (1927) 624; that the closed subsets of a closure operator are those fixed by it and that a sublattice image is an interval condition is the standard order theory. That whether a selection rule can be imposed on Λ₉ with E = 0 is decided by whether its set is convex in the range of its defining quantity — the spin diagonal convex and holding at four caps, the parity rule punctured at zero and closing to E = 750, with the repair named as moving the hole to an endpoint — is this book's.**

### Which selection rules a closed index will accept

**A cell of Λ is an electromagnetic transition, and the rules that decide whether a photon connects two configurations — multipole, parity, the change in spin — are not coordinates of Λ but functions of the coordinates it already carries. The index therefore imposes no electromagnetic constraint of its own; the question is only which of those rules it will hold once they are handed to it. A selection rule presented as a set of admissible cells may be imposed on Λ₉ with closure surviving exactly when that set is convex in the range of the quantity defining it, which is §17.3's criterion arriving where it can be measured. The spin rule ΔS = 0 is the diagonal of a difference, σ⁻¹({0}), and a diagonal is two monotone one-parent bounds at once; it is convex in range, and imposing it keeps 526 of Λ₉'s 1,654 cells at defect zero, holding not at one cap but at four settings of §7.4 — 1,654, 2,664, 44,153 and 60,164 cells, E = 0 at each. The parity rule |Δℓ| = 1 is δ⁻¹({−1, +1}), and here the set has a hole: it admits Δℓ = −1 and Δℓ = +1 and refuses the Δℓ = 0 between them, so it is not convex in range, and imposing it keeps 840 cells at a defect of 750 — the closure of the punctured set fills the hole straight back in. The two rules divide on exactly the property the criterion names, and the criterion says which in advance rather than after the count. The parity rule is a further instance of the congruence form of Three excluded forms (§12.11.2) — a bound with a fixed parity between admissible values — and it is the first for which the criterion also names the repair that would work: any reparametrisation that moves the hole to an endpoint of the range makes the set convex and closes it, at the cost of no longer being the parity rule. So one of the two electromagnetic rules can be carried by the index at E = 0 and the other cannot, and the line between them is not physical but order-theoretic: a rule is admissible when its image is an interval, and refused when its image is an interval with a point removed.**

*the spin rule σ⁻¹({0}) imposed on Λ₉, 526 cells at E = 0 and stable across the four caps 1,654 / 2,664 / 44,153 / 60,164 (the four-cap sizes carried from the record); the parity rule δ⁻¹({−1, +1}) imposed on Λ₉, 840 cells at E = 750; convexity-in-range read on Δℓ = f − ℓ and ΔS = 2S′ − 2S, at the caps of §7.4, (n, e, ℓ, k, f) = (3, 3, 1, 3, 1).*

Proved — M §12.11.8, §17.3; Russell & Saunders 1925; Laporte 1924; Wigner 1927.

> **Prior art: that the electric-dipole spin rule is ΔS = 0 in LS coupling is Russell & Saunders, Astrophys. J. 61 (1925) 38, and that the parity rule is |Δℓ| = 1 is Laporte, Z. Phys. 23 (1924) 135, its group-theoretic ground Wigner, Z. Phys. 43 (1927) 624; that the closed subsets of a closure operator are those fixed by it, so that admissibility is an interval condition on the defining quantity, is the standard order theory. That whether a selection rule can be imposed on Λ₉ with E = 0 is decided by whether its set is convex in the range of its defining quantity — the spin diagonal convex and holding at four caps, the parity rule punctured at zero and closing to E = 750, the repair being to move the hole to an endpoint — is this book's.**
EOF

**### Four coupling schemes price four routes to one object**

**A coupling scheme is a basis change, and the atom does not move under it, so the four standard schemes for a two-electron configuration must agree on the physics and may disagree only on the bookkeeping — and measured against Λ₁₃ they do exactly that. The tower as built uses jK, and its cell count is 199,130; rebuilding LK from its recoupling chain reproduces its stated figure from the chain alone at 341,150. LS and jj depend on a looseness convention that the physics names but does not fix a value for, and two committed readings of it bracket rather than determine their counts: LS falls in [383,065, 597,325] and contains 431,050, jj in [160,380, 244,060] and contains 206,520. The four counts span a factor of 2.17, and that spread is the whole point: it prices four routes to one object, not four objects. Where the counts differ the exact J multiset does not, and this is the proof and not a coincidence of the sample: a coupling scheme is a unitary change of basis on the same space, so the multiset of total J it yields is invariant under recoupling — the same whether J is reached through K or directly. The fifteen configurations computed through the jK, LS and jj chains independently are the witness, identical in every one, and §12.11.4 states the same at the channel level, 12 of 12 (J_c, f) pairs, while the envelopes differ, 64.4 per cent through K against 39.4 direct. The envelope does not commute with recoupling though the multiset does; the index remembers the route and the atom does not. One route is then privileged, and here for a structural reason rather than a proved one: because the outer electron's spin is a half, the final triangle degenerates to the mutual bound |2J − 2K| ≤ 1, which is admissible on both sides and closes, losing only the parity point 2J = 2K — the smallest quantum of angular momentum being the largest the constraint language can hold exactly, and the scheme that reaches it is jK, which the atoms of the later chapters realise at high n because the weak coupling goes last. [The jK privilege is interpretation; the multiset invariance and the four counts are proved and measured.]**

*jK = 199,130 as |Λ₁₃| measured on the rebuilt tower at the caps of §7.4, (n, e, ℓ, k, f) = (3, 3, 1, 3, 1); LK = 341,150, the LS bracket [383,065, 597,325] ∋ 431,050 and the jj bracket [160,380, 244,060] ∋ 206,520, and the 15-of-15 identity of the J multiset across schemes, from the record; the 2.17-fold spread and the 64.4-against-39.4 envelope contrast as §12.11.4.*

Proved — M §12.11.8, §12.11.4; Racah 1942; Cowan & Andrew 1965.

> **Prior art: that jK, LK, LS and jj are the four types of pure coupling for a two-electron configuration is Cowan & Andrew, J. Opt. Soc. Am. 55 (1965) 502 — a precedent for the set and not only for its members — and the recoupling algebra by which a scheme is a change of basis is Racah, Phys. Rev. 62 (1942) 438. That the four schemes reproduce or bracket the Λ₁₃ counts — jK 199,130, LK 341,150, LS ∋ 431,050, jj ∋ 206,520, a 2.17-fold spread — while the exact J multiset is identical across all four in fifteen of fifteen configurations, so that the cell-count spread prices four routes to one object and jK is privileged by the outer electron's half-spin degenerating the final triangle to |2J − 2K| ≤ 1, is this book's.**

**MC-39 — "Adjunction never repairs a closed index"** (§17.2, **Proved**)

> **A non-closed index cannot be mended by adding a coordinate that is a function of the ones it already has, and the proof is one line. Adjoin to a set S a coordinate h computed from each cell, forming the graph S′ = {(x, h(x))}; then the join of (x, h(x)) and (y, h(y)) is (x ∨ y, h(x) ∨ h(y)), and if S′ is closed that pair lies in S′, so x ∨ y lies in S — and meets likewise. So S′ closed forces S closed: the graph of a derived coordinate can be closed only if its base already was. The contrapositive is the working statement — a set that is not closed stays not closed under the adjunction of any function of its coordinates — and it fixes what adjunction can be for. ### Adjunction never repairs a closed index

**A non-closed index cannot be mended by adding a coordinate that is a function of the ones it already has, and the proof is one line. Adjoin to a set S a coordinate h computed from each cell, forming the graph S′ = {(x, h(x))}; then the join of (x, h(x)) and (y, h(y)) is (x ∨ y, h(x) ∨ h(y)), and if S′ is closed that pair lies in S′, so x ∨ y lies in S — and meets likewise. So S′ closed forces S closed: the graph of a derived coordinate can be closed only if its base already was. The contrapositive is the working statement — a set that is not closed stays not closed under the adjunction of any function of its coordinates — and it fixes what adjunction can be for. The companion criterion says which coordinates close at all: Λ × h is closed exactly when h is a lattice homomorphism, and that was measured across four hundred and twenty-four tests at a hundred per cent — projections, minima and constants qualify, sums, products and differences do not. A difference fails for the reason the join exposes: over x ∨ y the two terms take their maxima independently, so e(x∨y) − ℓ(x∨y) need not equal the larger of the two differences, and the graph breaks. This is why the electromagnetic coordinates cannot improve Λ: every one of them is a function of coordinates Λ already carries, and adjoining them gives not repair but E = 3,900, the worked instance of the theorem in the direction that a derived coordinate strictly worsens closure rather than improving it. Only three routes to repair remain, and the theorem is what leaves exactly three: enlarge the index by adding cells, restrict it by removing them, or reorder it and change neither — adjoining a derived axis is none of these, and is ruled out at the source.**

*the theorem proved by the join/meet identity on the graph {(x, h(x))}; the homomorphism criterion Λ × h closed ⟺ h a lattice homomorphism measured at 100 % over 424 tests, projections/minima/constants qualifying and sums/products/differences not, confirmed on the rebuilt Λ₈ for the projection, minimum, constant and difference cases; the E = 3,900 electromagnetic adjunction as the worked instance, at the caps of §7.4, (n, e, ℓ, k, f) = (3, 3, 1, 3, 1).*

Proved — M §17.2; Birkhoff 1940.

That a non-closed index therefore cannot be repaired by adjoining any function of its own coordinates, leaving only enlarge, restrict and reorder as repairs, and that the electromagnetic coordinates are the worked instance at E = 3,900, is this book's.**

So S′ closed forces S closed: the graph of a derived coordinate can be closed only if its base already was. The contrapositive is the working statement — a set that is not closed stays not closed under the adjunction of any function of its coordinates — and it fixes what adjunction can be for. The companion criterion says which coordinates close at all: Λ × h is closed exactly when h is a lattice homomorphism, and that was measured across four hundred and twenty-four tests at a hundred per cent — projections, minima and constants qualify, sums, products and differences do not. A difference fails for the reason the join exposes: over x ∨ y the two terms take their maxima independently, so e(x∨y) − ℓ(x∨y) need not equal the larger of the two differences, and the graph breaks. Good question — let me check whether the calendar actually belongs, rather than defend it because §21.1 lists it.

The calendar (365 days, E=7 as drawn vs E=0 by length) is one of §21.1's eight rows, and it's a legitimate *instance* of the general pattern: one object, two coordinate systems, E measuring the translation cost. In that narrow sense it "fits."

But your question cuts to whether it's *relevant to MC-40 specifically*, and there's a real distinction. MC-40 is a **Mathematical Compendium** entry justifying the book's subtitle — the claim that the method's languages speak to one another via ℛ. The instances that carry that claim are the ones about **Λ and the method's own objects**: the periodic table (the subject), the parity rule (Λ₉), the J multiset (the tower), slack (Λ's void/order/calculus identity), and Λ at 976 in six languages. Those are the method demonstrating translation-cost *on its own material*.

The calendar is different in kind: it's an **external illustration** — an everyday index (months) used to show that E-under-recoordinatisation is a general phenomenon, not special to Λ. It's pedagogically apt in the main-volume §21.1, where the point is partly "this pattern is everywhere." But in a compendium entry whose job is the subtitle's justification — that *the transitions* speak the languages — the calendar is a borrowed example, not part of the object the compendium indexes. It proves the pattern is general; it doesn't advance the claim about Λ.

So the calendar's relevance to MC-40 is weaker than the other five. It's not wrong — it's genuinely one of the eight and genuinely an instance — but it's the one row that's about *something other than the method's own objects*, which is why it stands out in a compendium entry.

I'm not going to cut it on my own read, because "belongs in the subtitle-justification entry" versus "is a valid §21.1 instance" is an editorial call, and the calendar does legitimately appear in the source table. But I'll put the question to you plainly: should MC-40 drop the calendar and stand on the five instances drawn from the method's own objects (periodic table, parity, J multiset, slack, Λ-at-976), or keep it as §21.1 has it?

The index therefore imposes no electromagnetic constraint of its own; the question is only which of those rules it will hold once they are handed to it. A selection rule presented as a set of admissible cells may be imposed on Λ₉ with closure surviving exactly when that set is convex in the range of the quantity defining it, which is §17.3's criterion arriving where it can be measured. The spin rule ΔS = 0 is the diagonal of a difference, σ⁻¹({0}), and a diagonal is two monotone one-parent bounds at once; it is convex in range, and imposing it keeps 526 of Λ₉'s 1,654 cells at defect zero, holding not at one cap but at four settings of §7.4 — 1,654, 2,664, 44,153 and 60,164 cells, E = 0 at each. The parity rule |Δℓ| = 1 is δ⁻¹({−1, +1}), and here the set has a hole: it admits Δℓ = −1 and Δℓ = +1 and refuses the Δℓ = 0 between them, so it is not convex in range, and imposing it keeps 840 cells at a defect of 750 — the closure of the punctured set fills the hole straight back in. The two rules divide on exactly the property the criterion names, and the criterion says which in advance rather than after the count. The parity rule is a further instance of the congruence form of Three excluded forms (§12.11.2) — a bound with a fixed parity between admissible values — and it is the first for which the criterion also names the repair that would work: any reparametrisation that moves the hole to an endpoint of the range makes the set convex and closes it, at the cost of no longer being the parity rule. So one of the two electromagnetic rules can be carried by the index at E = 0 and the other cannot, and the line between them is not physical but order-theoretic: a rule is admissible when its image is an interval, and refused when its image is an interval with a point removed.**

### The multipole is fixed by the orbital jump and the parity, and nothing else the index carries

**Whether a photon connects two configurations is decided by its multipolarity, and the multipole is fixed by two things a transition carries in Λ — the change in orbital angular momentum and the parity of the jump — with the change in total J, which would ordinarily complete the rule, unavailable at any level of the tower. The assignment is the lowest multipole whose parity matches: Δℓ = 0 gives a magnetic dipole M1, Δℓ = 1 an electric dipole E1, Δℓ = 2 an electric quadrupole E2, Δℓ = 3 an octupole E3. **PC-03 — "The four coupling schemes as physical recoupling chains"** (§12.11.8, Computed)

> **A coupling scheme is an order in which the four angular momenta of a two-electron configuration — the two orbital momenta and the two spins — are added. Four orders are standard. In jK the inner electron's orbital and spin couple first to j₁, then the outer orbital joins to give K, then the outer spin gives J: ℓ₁ + s₁ = j₁, j₁ + ℓ₂ = K, K + s₂ = J. In LK the two orbital momenta couple to L, then the core spin joins to give K, then the outer spin gives J. In LS the two orbital momenta couple to L and the two spins to S, and L and S give J. In jj each electron's orbital and spin couple to a j, and the two j's give J. The schemes are physical, not notational: each applies where its couplings are the strong ones. LS holds when the electrostatic term dominates and spin-orbit is weak; jj when spin-orbit dominates; jK when the outer electron is loosely bound and its own spin-orbit coupling is the weakest interaction present, coupled last. In jK the inner electron's orbital and spin couple first to j₁, then the outer orbital joins to give K, then the outer spin gives J: ℓ₁ + s₁ = j₁, j₁ + ℓ₂ = K, K + s₂ = J. In LK the two orbital momenta couple to L, then the core spin joins to give K, then the outer spin gives J. In LS the two orbital momenta couple to L and the two spins to S, and L and S give J. In jj each electron's orbital and spin couple to a j, and the two j's give J. The schemes are physical, not notational: each applies where its couplings are the strong ones. LS holds when the electrostatic term dominates and spin-orbit is weak; jj when spin-orbit dominates; jK when the outer electron is loosely bound and its own spin-orbit coupling is the weakest interaction present, coupled last. That is why jK is the scheme high Rydberg states realise — the weak coupling goes last, and for a distant outer electron the weakest coupling is its spin to the rest. jK carries a further advantage in this index: because the outer electron's spin is ½, the final triangle K + s₂ = J degenerates to |2J − 2K| ≤ 1, a mutual bound that closes, so jK reaches an exact bound where the others do not. Cowan and Andrew treat exactly these four as the pure coupling types for two-electron configurations.**

*the four recoupling chains — jK (ℓ₁+s₁=j₁, j₁+ℓ₂=K, K+s₂=J), LK, LS, jj — with the physical regime each applies in and the ½-spin degeneracy giving jK its exact final bound |2J − 2K| ≤ 1; the chain definitions from NIST and the four-scheme precedent from the record, at the caps of §7.4, (n, e, ℓ, k, f) = (3, 3, 1, 3, 1).*

Computed — M §12.11.8; Racah 1942; Cowan & Andrew 1965.

> **Prior art: the recoupling algebra by which a coupling scheme is a change of basis is Racah, Phys. Rev. 62 (1942) 438, and the four schemes jK, LK, LS, jj are the pure coupling types for a two-electron configuration — Cowan & Andrew, J. Opt. Soc. Am. 55 (1965) 502. That jK is the scheme high Rydberg states realise, the weak coupling going last, and that its outer ½-spin degenerates the final triangle to |2J − 2K| ≤ 1, an exact bound, is this book's reading.**
EOF

That's real, and it's the semiclassical picture *behind* why the couplings have the strengths they do. But it is not what PC-03 states. PC-03 states which momenta couple first, i.e. which precession is fast (tightly coupled) and which is slow (loosely coupled) — the *ordering* of the couplings by strength — without describing the precession itself.

So the honest distinction:

- **What PC-03 says:** the four momenta add in a scheme-dependent order; jK adds the outer spin last because it's the weakest coupling. This is kinematics of angular-momentum addition.
